implementation_notes: ActiveModel/ActiveRecord ships the projection: as_json(only: [...], except: [...], methods: [...], include: {assoc: {only: ...}}) limits the emitted attributes and recurses into associations, so a Rails controller implements partial responses in one line. Validate the names against the model's attribute vocabulary first - the option itself ignores names it does not recognise - and remember that as_json still builds the full attribute hash before filtering.
code_sketch:
FIELDS = %w[id email created_at].freeze

def show
  requested = params[:fields]&.split(",") || FIELDS
  unknown = requested - FIELDS
  return render(json: { error: "unknown fields: #{unknown}" }, status: :bad_request) if unknown.any?

  render json: User.find(params[:id]).as_json(only: requested)
end
pitfalls: only: silently ignores unknown attribute names, so a typo shrinks the payload instead of raising - validate against attribute_names (or a constant) at the boundary.
as_json allocates the complete attribute hash (serializable_hash) before the filter applies, which is wasted work for slim views over large models.
Version drift: Rails' serialization defaults (include_root_in_json, key transforms) changed across majors, so the same as_json(only:) call can produce a different envelope after an upgrade.
Deep include:/only: hashes are easy to get subtly wrong (an association excluded only two levels down), and nothing in the type system checks them.

variants.name: jsonapi-serializer sparse fieldsets
variants.implementation_notes: The jsonapi-serializer gem implements JSON:API sparse fieldsets: pass fields: { user: [:id, :email] } and the serializer returns only those attributes for that type, per type and per relationship, which is what the fields[TYPE] query parameter in the JSON:API spec describes. It also folds the fieldset into the cache namespace when caching is enabled, so different selections do not collide - a detail hand-rolled projections usually get wrong.
variants.code_sketch:
def show
  fields = { user: (params.dig(:fields, :user)&.split(",") || %w[id email]) }
  record = User.find(params[:id])
  render json: UserSerializer.new(record, { fields: fields }).serializable_hash
end
pitfalls: The gem's contract is JSON:API's (fields[TYPE]), so the field names are the serializer's attribute names - renaming an attribute is a breaking API change.
Sparse fieldsets combine with includes: a relationship that is not selected still needs the serializer definition, and the two options can fight over what the document contains.
Caching keys grow with the fieldset (by design), so a caller can multiply cache entries by enumerating selections unless fields are validated against the serializer vocabulary.
